Observations with an X-ray telescope over three epochs show that the star's X-ray luminosity varies by a factor of about forty on timescales of days. Spectral fitting of the brightest epoch requires a hot thermal component at roughly 30 million kelvin, consistent with magnetically confined plasma, plus a harder tail suggestive of flaring. The outbursts are not periodic, which argues against an orbiting companion as the trigger. Instead, the light curve resembles those of young, rapidly rotating stars in which magnetic reconnection events heat coronal loops. Optical spectra taken within a week of the peak show strong emission in hydrogen lines, supporting the interpretation that accretion from a surrounding disk may also contribute. Further monitoring is planned to separate these mechanisms.
